title: Sam Altman says AI means we can no longer just patch all the bugs
excerpt: Sam Altman told Stanford students we can no longer patch all the bugs as AI finds them, and called for an AI defence shield. He also spoke on pacing.
content_html:
Sam Altman says patching software flaws one by one will no longer keep up with AI-driven attacks. The OpenAI chief executive spoke to students at Stanford Graduate School of Business last week. Defenders will need a new kind of shield, he said, built with the same AI.

“I no longer think we’re going to be able to just patch all the bugs. I think we’re going to have to completely switch the defense model to sort of using the same technology for sort of a new kind of defense shield.” Sam Altman, OpenAI

He spoke in a View From The Top interview with MBA student Claudia Chen, which the school has published on YouTube. The comments came in the week of the PHP2Shell flaws, which researchers found with the help of AI.

‘Somewhat astonished’

Asked what business leaders should do about AI’s risks, Altman picked cybersecurity. He said organisations, countries and individuals still have not taken the threat seriously.

He pointed back to what he called “the Mythos freakout” earlier this year. People patched some bugs then, he said, but assumed the models had found everything they ever would. Most leaders have “somewhat moved on”, while the models kept improving.

“I think it’s a huge safety and security issue, and I am somewhat astonished at how relatively little attention it’s getting.” Sam Altman

His company has had its own problems with security. That same week, OpenAI said it now trains frontier models offline, after its agents broke out of test environments.

Slowing down, and open weights

Altman also said the past six months had tested his convictions. In mathematical reasoning, he said, OpenAI already has superintelligence “in some narrow senses”.

“We’re going to have to make some changes to how we think about pacing progress from here.” Sam Altman

Alignment, meaning whether a model acts in line with human interests, has so far been easier than he expected. He warned that this may not last. Some AI efforts around the world are so confident in alignment that they are “too willing to run ahead”, he said.

On open-weight models, he said society needs them up to a fairly high level of capability. But he said OpenAI could not responsibly release the weights of its best internal model “anytime soon”.

Jobs, maths and chips

Altman said he does not expect “a job apocalypse”, though many tasks and some kinds of jobs will change. He described mathematicians moving from “we’re cooked” to planning new kinds of careers within days of OpenAI’s maths results.

Asked where OpenAI is investing next, he named robots that can build more robots. He also described data centres that could, in effect, build more data centres. He also named the company’s own Jalapeño chip and its successor, and the wider supply chain of fabs, power and equipment.
